topic.name: Finding Intersections of Parametric Curves and Lines

question.text: Find the values of $t$ at which the curve $x=-t^2,y=-3t$ intersects the line $x-y+4=0,$ as shown above.
question.explanation:
Notice that the line and curve intersect twice, so we are expecting two solutions.

To find the coordinates of the intersection points, we take the equation of the line, replace $x$ and $y$ with the parametric formulas, and then solve for $t.$ \[ \begin{align} x-y+4 &= 0\\[3pt] (-t^2) - (-3t) + 4&=0\\[3pt] -t^2 + 3t +4 &=0\\[3pt] -(t+1)(t-4) &=0\\[3pt] t&=-1,4. \end{align} \]

example.title: Finding the Intersection of a Parametric Curve and a Line

question.text: Find the values of $\theta$ at which the curve $x=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos\theta,y=2\sin\theta,0\leq \theta < 2\pi$ intersects the line $x-y=0.$
question.explanation:
To find the coordinates of the points of intersection, we take the equation of the line, replace $x$ and $y$ with the parametric formulas, and then solve for $\theta.$ \[ \begin{align} x-y&= 0\\[5pt] \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos\theta - 2\sin\theta &=0\\[5pt] \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos\theta & = 2\sin\theta \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\cos\theta&=\sin\theta\\[5pt] \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sqrt{3} \cos\theta}&=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\\[5pt] \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\[5pt] \tan\theta&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{3}. \end{align} \]

The principal value of $\theta$ is

\[ \theta = \arctan\left(\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}. \]

This value lies inside the domain $0\leq \theta < 2\pi,$ so our first solution is $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

To get a second solution, we add $\pi$ to $\theta_1\mathbin{:}$

\[ \theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \pi = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \]

Therefore, our solutions are $\dfrac{\pi}{6},\,\dfrac{7\pi}{6}.$

example.title: Finding the Intersection of a Trigonometric Parametric Curve and a Line

question.text: Find the points where the curve $x = t^2, \, y = 4t$ intersects the line $x + y + 3 = 0.$
question.explanation:
To find the coordinates of intersection points, we take the equation of the line, replace $x$ and $y$ with the parametric formulas, and then solve for $t.$ Upon finding $t,$ we then find the coordinates of the intersection points. \begin{align} x + y + 3 &= 0\\[5pt] t^2 + 4t + 3 &= 0\\[5pt] (t+3)(t+1) &=0\\[5pt] t&=-3,-1. \end{align} Now that we have the values of $t,$ we proceed to find $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

  • We start with $t=-3.$ For $x,$ we have \begin{align} x &= t^2\\[5pt] &= (-3)^2\\[5pt] &=9. \end{align} For $y,$ we have \begin{align} y &= 4t \\[5pt] &= 4(-3) \\[5pt] &=-12. \end{align} So, the coordinates of the first intersection point are $(9,-12).$

  • We now move over to $t=-1.$ For $x,$ we have \begin{align} x &= t^2 \\[5pt] &= (-1)^2 \\[5pt] &= 1. \end{align} For $y,$ we have \begin{align} y &= 4t \\[5pt] &= 4(-1) \\[5pt] &= -4. \end{align} So, the coordinates of the second intersection point are $(1,-4).$

Therefore, the curve $x= t^2,y= 4t$ intersects the line $x + y + 3 =0$ at the points $(1,\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{-4})$ and $(\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{9},\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{-12}).$

question.text: In ascending order, the values of $t$ at which the curve $x = t + 4,\,y = \dfrac{1}{2}t^2 - 3$ intersects the line $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x - 2$ (shown above) are
question.explanation:
Notice that the line and curve intersect twice, so we expect two solutions.

To find the coordinates of the intersection points, we take the equation of the line, replace $x$ and $y$ with the parametric formulas, and then solve for $t.$ \begin{align} y &= \dfrac{1}{2}x - 2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{1}{2}t^2 - 3 &= \dfrac{1}{2}(t+4) - 2 \\[5pt] t^2 - 6 &= (t+4) - 4 \\[5pt] t^2 - 6 &= t \\[5pt] t^2 - t - 6 &= 0 \\[5pt] (t+2)(t-3) &= 0 \\[5pt] t &= -2,\, 3. \end{align}

Therefore, in ascending order, the values of $t$ where the curve $x = t + 4,\,y = \dfrac{1}{2}t^2 - 3$ intersects the line $y = \dfrac{1}{2}x - 2$ are $t = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{-2}$ and $t = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{3}.$

example.title: Finding the Intersection of a Parametric Curve and a Line

question.text: In ascending order, the values of $\theta$ at which the curve $x=2\cos\theta, \, y=\sin\theta, \, 0\leq \theta < 2\pi$ intersects the line $2\sqrt{3}\,y = x$ are
question.explanation:
To find the coordinates of the points of intersection, we take the equation of the line, replace $x$ and $y$ with the parametric formulas, and then solve for $\theta.$

\begin{align} 2\sqrt{3}\,y &= x \\[5pt] 2\sqrt{3}\,\sin\theta &= 2\cos\theta \\[5pt] \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}\,\sin\theta}{2\sqrt{3}\cos\theta} &= \dfrac{2\cos\theta}{2\sqrt{3}\cos\theta} \\[5pt] \tan\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}. \end{align}

The principal value of $\theta$ is \[ \theta = \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt 3}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{6}. \]

This value lies inside the domain $0\leq \theta < 2\pi,$ so our first solution is $\theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

To get a second solution, we add $\pi$ to $\theta_1\mathbin{:}$ \[ \theta_1 = \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \pi = \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \]

Therefore, in ascending order, our solutions are $\theta = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{\pi}{6}}$ and $\theta = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid gainsboro]{\dfrac{7\pi}{6}}.$
